item.title: Tight hug after 27 years: Reunion across ocean, marking China-US folk friendship
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 23:54:00
American teacher Ronald Sakolsky reunites with desert fighter Yin Yuzhen at an airport in Ordos, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region on August 23, 2026. Photo: Xinhua A long-awaited reunion that captured wide public attention unfolded on Sunday evening when American teacher Ronald Sakolsky and Yin Yuzhen, a model worker renowned for planting trees and combating desertification, reunited and embraced tearfully with overwhelming emotion at an airport in Ordos, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, after 27 years of separation across the ocean. The reunion began with a single act of generosity in 1999. When Sakolsky arrived in China as a participant in a China-US education exchange program, he was moved by Yin and her husband's tireless efforts to curb desertification in the Mu Us Desert in Inner Mongolia. He raised $5,000 to fund their local tree-planting initiative. The young saplings they bought with the donation have since matured into more than 50,000 full-grown trees, transforming the once desolate, sandy wasteland into a thriving green landscape. This hug, transcending time and distance, marked not only friendship between the two countries, but also showcased the sincerity of Chinese people and a green miracle made possible through continuous joint efforts. Hug across 27 years At 2:48 am on early Sunday morning, Ronald Sakolsky arrived at Beijing Capital International Airport after over 10 hours of flight. As he stepped into the arrivals hall, he greeted the waiting reporters with earnest Putonghua "Wo hui lai le," meaning "I'm back." "When I saw the lights in Beijing as we were landing is when I realized that I am back in my second home." Asked what he is most looking forward to about this journey, Sakolsky told the Global Times that "I want to see Ms Yin, see the forests, see the students I have not seen for almost 30 years, my colleagues. I want to see the Chinese people." He then flew to Ordos for the meeting with his desert reclamation partner. Yin waited at the arrival gate at the airport in Ordos very early, murmuring English sentence she particularly learned for this occasion - "Welcome to China, my brother." Her eyes were fixed on the escalator and she wiped away her tears multiple times during the wait, the Global Times reporter observed. Sakolsky said in earlier interview with the Global Times that he was looking forward to this reunion and could not hold his tears back when he thought of the moment. He was about to give Yin a hug when they meet. When Sakolsky finally appeared in front of Yin, their eyes welled up. Stepping off the elevator, Sakolsky could barely contain his excitement, muttering "Oh my God, oh my God." They hurried toward each other and locked in a tight embrace at last - the long-awaited hug 27 years in the making. "This is a dream come true, from a lady who is the hero of the story, not me," Sakolsky told the Global Times at the airport, barely holding his emotion. "She made a promise 27 years ago, and she kept her promise." Talking about his donation almost three decades ago, Sakolsky said the purpose was to help her, "because she was beautifying the motherland." Now, in response to an invitation to return to China for a trip to see the green planting from his donation and to returning to the city of Luoyang, Central China's Henan Province, where he taught in the exchange program for several years, Sakolsky noted that "China had done so much for me that I wanted to say thank you to China." A return of kindness For this reunion after 27 years, Yin had carefully prepared. Steamed buns, meaning "upward," fresh vegetables and fruits picked in the land transformed from desert. Yin, never familiar with any foreign language, learned some English phrases, including "welcome to China" she practiced, "my brother" to greet Sakolsky, and "more, more" to persuade the American friend to eat more. On Sunday, Yin did her hair and wore a red scarf alongside an outfit with a green shade, which she picked particularly for the reunion, as "green is the color of the Earth," as she told the Global Times. Yin is not the only old friend that was looking forward to the reunion. While Sakolsky was still on his over-10-hour flight from the US to Beijing, Bai Fan was also on the way - driving over 850 kilometers from Luoyang to Inner Mongolia. The journey would take a day and a half. Bai was the vice principal of Luoyang Foreign Language School, overseeing international affairs. Sakolsky was an exchange teacher there through a China-US program, and was Bai's "neighbor right across the hall." Why drive such a distance? Bai had prepared special cultural gifts - peony porcelain and Hanguan Kiln purple clay tea ware, distinctive local handicrafts that proved too bulky and fragile for air travel or high-speed rail. Bai recalled Sakolsky's continuous interest in Chinese culture, and sending a replica of Terracotta Warriors to the US at Sakolsky's request. "I hope he can take these Luoyang elements and Chinese symbols to the world," Bai told the Global Times in a phone interview on Sunday. Bai is also eager to see Sakolsky at a place that they had traveled together 27 years ago. When Sakolsky came to Luoyang for the exchange program, Bai was his designated liaison. Together, they traveled to the heart of the Mu Us Desert to deliver the $5,000 donation. Bai still vividly remembers the desolate desert back then, where finger-thin saplings were watered ladle by ladle by Yin. At that time, Sakolsky had constant concerns about whether the tiny saplings could survive in the wasteland, which makes today's sprawling 50,000-tree forest even more miraculous. The changed and unchanged Things have changed over the past 27 years. While waiting for Sakolsky, Yin jokingly said he got less hair, and she would not be able to recognize him if running up to him on street. The passage of time has brought far more than personal aging, according to Bai, another witness to the decades-long changes. "Everyone is growing older. Our families have expanded with more children, local communities have grown in population, and the surrounding environment is constantly evolving, just as our cities are undergoing profound transformations." On a night tour in Ordos on Sunday, Sakolsky, watching a fountain light show, said that "it is a 21st century city, but it looks like a 22nd century city. In the 2000s, Chinese government made a promise to Chinese people to beatify this country, and they succeeded." For Sakolsky, probably the most profound transformation lies in the depth of his human connection forged. "27 years ago, we were just friends and acquaintances. We are brother and sister now. So much has happened since then, but the important thing is many people have seen the story and now they can also help to make China beautiful," he told the reporters. Through joint efforts of people like Yin, the Mu Us Desert has turned from wasteland into a green oasis. China has contributed about 25 percent of the world's newly added green areas and taken the lead in achieving zero growth in land degradation, per official data. Meanwhile, there are things unchanged, including a vintage photo of the three standing in the desert that has decorated Bai's office through all these years - a permanent reminder of their original aspiration. This reunion will witness them retake the classic photo and plant new saplings together, expanding their green mission.

item.title: Canada launches a 'Chinese-styled counterattack' – a heavy blow: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 23:49:00
This combination of pictures created on August 22, 2026 shows US President Donald Trump in Washington, DC, on July 13, 2026 and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on August 22, 2026. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced retaliatory tariffs on the United States on August 22, after walking away from a "bad deal" on trade in a deepening rift between the longtime allies. Photo: VCG In the face of Washington's tariff stick, Canada has launched a "Chinese-styled counterattack": responding firmly and proportionally; defending sovereignty without compromise; and resorting to rules and legitimate countermeasures. As one of America's former closest allies, Canada's move reflects an increasingly clear consensus: No country has the privilege to monopolize the rules or dictate the fate of others. Washington probably never imagined that Ottawa would launch a "Chinese-styled counterattack." In response to the US 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced in a televised national address on Saturday that Canada would "match Washington's new tariffs dollar for dollar." Starting September 8, Canada will impose retaliatory tariffs on US sectors such as steel, dairy, home appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. Canada, a member of the Five Eyes alliance and NATO, has now dared to turn against Washington and respond with retaliatory tariffs. The significance of this move goes far beyond the scope of a North American trade dispute. The US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer disparagingly likened Canada's retaliation to "the kind of things that China would do." In an interview with US media, he claimed that after Washington introduced trade policies aimed at bringing production back home and protecting American jobs, "two countries in the world have retaliated against us: [the] People's Republic of China and Canada." China and Canada are the only countries daring to respond to US pressure with reciprocal measures. This indicates that the so-called "Chinese-styled counterattack" is, in fact, another term for "refusing to accept unilateral pressure." Canada's response offers the world a glimpse of what China has long stood for: responding firmly and proportionally; defending sovereignty without compromise; and resorting to rules and legitimate countermeasures. More accurately, this is not a uniquely Chinese approach, but rather the most fundamental principle of reciprocity in international trade. Canada's adoption of this path is no surprise. It is a legitimate response to unilateral bullying - raising a shield when faced with pressure. The "Chinese-styled counterattack" not only protects a country's own interests, but also safeguards the stability of global supply chains and the fairness of the international trading order. Canada's move shows that "strategic autonomy" is gradually evolving from a common aspiration of Global South countries into a real-world issue for US allies. More countries are realizing that concessions toward the US do not necessarily bring respect and stability, and only by having more partners, more markets and more room for independent choices can they gain the leverage for negotiation and the strength to protect themselves. Canada's decision to respond to the US in a "Chinese way" vividly illustrates a fact: In the face of a tariff stick, being an ally offers no "exemption." Today it is Canada; tomorrow it could be the EU, and the day after, Japan or South Korea. By listing China and Canada together as "retaliators," Greer acknowledges the failure of US policy - if the policy were truly "great," why would even one of its closest allies feel compelled to strike back? If a policy forces countries with different geopolitical positions and institutional systems to take countermeasures, then the question should not be "why are they acting like China," but rather "why is US policy producing more China-like responses." At a deeper level, Canada's "Chinese-styled counterattack" exposes the dilemma of unilateralism. Globalization is not a one-man show staged by the US, and industrial chains are deeply interconnected. The US wants to use tariff barriers to force production back home, yet ignores the basic economic factors of cost, efficiency and resource endowments. As one of the US largest trading partners, Canada sees hundreds and thousands of tons of goods crossing the border each day. In 2024, the two countries' average daily trade reached $2.5 billion, reflecting deeply integrated supply chains on both sides. By imposing tariffs, Washington is effectively cutting itself in the foot. Even Fox News, a conservative-leaning media outlet, published an article warning consumers that "your favorite cocktail could be an unexpected casualty of the trade fight," as Canadian whiskey is one of the commonly used base spirits for cocktails in US bars and restaurants. The so-called goal of "protecting American jobs" is, in plain terms, "America first, everyone else to the sidelines." And what has the result been? "First" has turned into isolation, and "bringing back" has turned into bleeding out. The so-called "correcting trade imbalances" has resulted in disrupted supply chains for domestic companies, with US ordinary consumers footing the bill and inflationary pressures remaining high. The US federal data shows that manufacturing companies reduced their workforce in each of the eight months that followed the "Liberation Day" tariffs. Even if tariff walls can "kill a thousand enemies," the self-inflicted damage is far from trivial. Canada's "Chinese-styled counterattack" is a heavy blow against protectionism. China's steadfast resistance to US unilateral tariffs was once described by some Western commentators as a "lone exception." Now that one of America's former closest allies has taken a similar path, this in itself is correcting the narrative over "who upholds the rules and who breaks them," while also demonstrating the necessity and legitimacy of China's reciprocal countermeasures. The essence of the "Chinese-styled counterattack" is an increasingly clear consensus: Openness must be built on equality, cooperation must be premised on mutual respect, and no country has the privilege to monopolize the rules or dictate the fate of others.

item.title: Can humanoid robots move beyond the games?
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 22:29:00
A Tien Kung robot (left) competes in the 400-meter race at the National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing on August 23, 2026 during the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games (WHRG). Photo: VCG On the blue track inside the National Speed Skating Oval, robots chased each other in the 400-meter race. A sprinting Tien Kung robot was tripped by a rival robot lying on the track but did not fall. Instead, it adjusted its posture in seconds and continued toward the finish line with a result of 38.15 seconds, breaking human 400-meter race world record of 43.03 seconds, held by South African athlete Wayde van Niekerk. This scene unfolded on Sunday, the first official competition day of the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games (WHRG). Later that evening, a humanoid robot named Lightning, developed by Honor Co., broke the long-standing human 1,500-meter world record of 3:26 set by Moroccan athlete Hicham El Guerrouj with a time of 2:30.22. Just one night earlier, during the opening ceremony's 100-meter sprint and high jump demonstrations, humanoid robots had already shattered records long held by human athletes Usain Bolt and Javier Sotomayor — merely an appetizer for the five-day sci-fi spectacle. The Games have attracted 666 teams from 16 countries across six continents, up 138 percent from its inaugural edition. The number of participating robots quadrupled to 2,056, the Global Times learned from the organizing committee. Yet the biggest change this year was not only the scale, but also the technological maturity. More teams have shifted from remote-controlled robots to fully autonomous systems. Chinese observers, after watching several events, said humanoid robots are no longer limited to simple demonstrations of walking or dancing. Increasingly, they are being tested in environments that demand speed, coordination, perception and decision-making. From movement to intelligence Behind the record-breaking performances are a series of technological upgrades. During the running events, Global Times reporters observed that robots were able to make subtle movements around their hip joints while walking, allowing them to maintain balance and produce movements closer to human biomechanics. Guo Yijie, technical director of Tien Kung Ultra, said the improvement came from advances in hardware design. "Robot joints have improved in torque and speed. As competitions demand higher power output, the reliability of the main control board, power board and high-power battery discharge capability have become increasingly important," Guo told the Global Times. According to Guo, the same Tien Kung Ultra robot was used in both sprinting and jumping events. For running, the waist needs rotation to balance the inertia generated by leg movements. For jumping, the upper body requires pitching movement to help the robot achieve greater distance or height, Guo said, noting that these can all be achieved with only slight adjustments to the waist configuration were needed, and it highly demonstrated to the robot design's flexibility. Besides the hardware upgrades, developments in robots' faster decision-making in "brains' is better showcased in football competitions. The Booster T2 robot used by many domestic and overseas football teams has increased its onboard computing capability by 10 times compared with the previous generation. The time from recognizing the goal to deciding whether to pass or shoot has been reduced to around 100 milliseconds - faster than the time humans usually need to blink. Cheng Hao, a technical representative from Boosters Robotics, said the improvement represents an "end-to-end" transformation in embodied intelligence. "In the past, robots relied on separate steps: perception, planning, decision-making and execution. Each stage was disconnected. Now, with an end-to-end motion foundation model, visual input can directly generate joint control commands," Cheng said. The newly introduced table tennis and tennis competitions are also testing another important capability: perception. "Robots are moving from simply recognizing the three-dimensional position of a ball to understanding the movement information of opponents and more complex environments," said Li Yinghui, a postdoc researcher and the leader from the Hong Kong University team at the table tennis event. Such capabilities developed in sports scenarios could eventually be transferred to other scenarios in industries or daily life, Li said. Beyond entertainment Though clips from the robot competitions have made a buzz on social media, with some critics from Western media questioning why robots need to dance, play football or compete in athletics while arguing that these activities appear far from everyday needs. Zhou Changjiu, Vice President of the RoboCup Federation and the Robotics Competition Association of the Asia-Pacific (RCAP), stressed robot sports are not designed for entertainment alone. "Robot competitions are testing the capabilities needed for humanoid robots to enter the real world," Zhou told the Global Times. Different events evaluate different abilities. Sprinting tests speed, marathons examine battery endurance and energy management, while football provides a comprehensive test because of its dynamic and unpredictable nature, testing intelligence, manipulation, interaction, safety, cost and trust at the same time, Zhou said. Unlike a single-task demonstration, football requires robots to cooperate. Players must understand their own roles, recognize teammates and opponents, and make collective decisions - a form of swarm intelligence that could become essential when robots work together in homes, factories and emergency rescue environments. Entertainment, however, can generate business opportunities. Gu Jinghai, brand director of EYOU Robot Co, told the Global Times that the company sold 95,000 integrated joints in China in 2025 and expects sales to exceed 1 million units in 2026. Growth mainly comes from planetary joints used in entertainment robots, while harmonic joints for industrial robots are also expanding steadily, he said. Jiao Jichao, an executive from UBTECH Robotics, said the criticism that "Chinese robots can only sing and dance" reflects only a temporary stage of development. "Performance and dancing are also real commercial demands, and their existence has value," Jiao said. "Beyond entertainment, Chinese robots are already demonstrating intelligent capabilities that support practical applications in manufacturing, and partnerships with companies including Huawei and Foxconn, where robots have already entered production lines in small-scale applications." The Outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan for National Economic and Social Development of China stated that the country will construct a comprehensive cultivation system for future industries including the embody intelligence as new economic growth drivers. Zhou said the development of humanoid robots is not only about individual machines, but about building an entire ecosystem. China's advantage lies in its complete supply chain, abundant application scenarios and manufacturing capabilities, while the fast growing industry still faces challenges such as the lack of unified standards. Gu said the company has launched mass production of robotics joint under domestic standard of auto parts. Robot competitions can help address these issues by creating common standards in areas such as competition rules, robot dimensions, communication systems, batteries and joint modules. "As applications expand, the cost of key robot components will continue to decline," Zhou said. "Numbers are magic," Zhou said. "If producing one robot costs a huge amount because it is handmade, producing one million robots will completely change the cost structure." For humanoid robots, the race taking place inside the Ice Ribbon may not ultimately be about who crosses the finish line first. It may be about whether these machines can learn to navigate the far more complicated race outside the stadium - the race into the real world.

item.title: GT Voice: Protectionism is the last thing European automakers need
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 21:46:00
Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT Sebastian Lechner, state chairperson of the Christian Democratic Union in Germany's Lower Saxony, has called for the EU to quickly impose import tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars, Reuters reported on Friday. For some time, European media have reported that the European Commission plans to impose countervailing duties on such vehicles, which will amplify concerns over China-EU trade tensions. As the home to Volkswagen's global headquarters, Lower Saxony has been bearing the brunt of industrial restructuring amid the global energy transition. So, the politician's call for imposing tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars is essentially an attempt to curry favor with local manufacturers and local workers in exchange for gaining political support from them. But turning the operational pressure of local carmakers into political demand to erect trade barriers will not solve Germany's industrial problems. On the contrary, protectionism will almost certainly steer German auto sector further down the wrong path. For years, a number of European politicians and industry players have attributed the rapid growth of Chinese new-energy vehicles to the so-called "subsidies," hoping that erecting higher tariffs can shield European carmakers from global competition. Yet, the growing popularity of Chinese hybrid vehicles in the European market stems from nothing but their perfect alignment with the most pressing consumer demands. For starters, it's very expensive for ordinary European consumers to replace vehicles due to the persistently high prices of local cars. The EU has unveiled a plan to drop the ban on new combustion-engine cars from 2035, which would allow continued sales of non-electric vehicles including plug‑in hybrids (PHEVs). Market acceptance of PHEVs is relatively high in Europe. As a matter of fact, Chinese PHEVs have helped fill a critical market gap and provided European consumers with a pragmatic and affordable low-carbon mobility solution. Resorting to protection by imposing higher trade tariffs will deprive European consumers of the right to buy high-quality and cost-effective cars. If anything, the market performance following the EU's imposition of new tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) has already proven that trade protectionism only delivers limited effects in the long run. A report published by The Guardian revealed this month that despite EU tariffs of up to 35.3 percent on the EVs made by some Chinese manufacturers, on top of the standard 10-percent import duty, Chinese EV sales have still risen across Europe to hit a record high. The share of EVs sold by Chinese brands rose to 14.2 percent across western European markets - or one in every seven EVs - in the first five months of this year, according to Schmidt Automotive Research. Following a brief sales drop caused by tariff shocks, Chinese cars have quickly regained growth momentum, as their appeal to European consumers who favor affordable, high‑quality electric mobility has not changed. If the EU extends protectionist measure to Chinese PHEVs, European consumers will bear the full brunt of higher prices. Elevated prices could erase the new energy consumption push in Europe. The European auto market, which has just begun to show signs of recovery, will once again be dragged into a prolonged slump by protectionism. According to China Automotive News, more than 40 percent of the complete vehicles exported from China to the EU market come from joint ventures or wholly foreign‑owned factories in China. That means for every five cars shipped to Europe, roughly two are produced by European or other foreign manufacturers - including BMW and Mercedes‑Benz, all of which rely on China's mature supply chains to build highly competitive models and ship them back to Europe. Imposing punitive duties on these vehicles would raise their costs and disrupt their integrated production strategies. In addition, China's stance on tackling trade issues with the EU has always been clear. In May, a spokesperson from China's Ministry of Commerce said that China will take resolute countermeasures if the EU insists on imposing discriminatory restrictions on Chinese companies. Ultimately, the competitiveness of the global auto industry is never decided by tariffs. The race toward electrification and intelligence is one of technological innovation, supply‑chain efficiency, and cost control. Tariff pushes by certain politicians may win favor from local workers, yet they will trap Europe's automotive industry in a vicious cycle of protectionism. In the long run, such short-sighted moves will undermine the long-term vitality and competitiveness of European carmakers.

item.title: F-16Vs headed to Taiwan region; expert says incapable of shifting cross-Straits air power balance
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 21:42:00
Illustration: Xia Qing/GT Recent media attention has focused on Taiwan region's purchase of 66 F-16V (Blk 70) fighter jets from the US, the first two of which are now en route to the island. A mainland expert said the induction of these jets cannot change the cross-Straits air power balance. Their performance is comparable to the PLA's J-10C, but against the likes of J-16, J-20 and J-35, their tactical value is limited. The real gap, however, is not in individual aircraft, but in the PLA's already mature air combat system. Taiwan region is beginning to receive the first operational aircraft from its 66-jet F-16V Block 70 order, reported Defence Security Asia on Saturday. The first two single-seat fighters, serials 6727 and 6728, departed the US on August 17, 2026, transited through Fort Worth and Hawaii, and were expected to continue through Guam before reaching Chihhang Air Base, weather permitting. In addition to purchasing brand-new fighters, Taiwan region had previously cooperated with the US to upgrade 140 F-16A/B aircraft to the F-16V (Blk 20) standard. That upgrade work was fully completed in December 2023, according to CNA on August 19. Taiwan region previously claimed that the F-16V (Blk 70), in addition to featuring increased thrust, airframe optimizations, extended range, and conformal fuel tanks, also enhances beyond-visual-range combat capability and partial stealth characteristics. It is equipped with an Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar, providing multiple functions including air-to-air search, tracking, weapons guidance, electronic warfare, and communications, according to the HK01. The F-16V (Blk 70) is the newest variant of the F-16 family, Song Zhongping, a mainland military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Sunday. The PLA's mainstay fighters have already been widely equipped with AESA radars and are at the same technological generation as the F-16V (Blk 70). In comparison with the J-10C, both fall into the light-to-medium fighter category and have a degree of comparability. However, comparing to a heavy fighter such as the J-16, and especially when facing fifth-generation aircraft like the J-20 and J-35 that possess a clear generational advantage, the F-16V has no edge at all. Constrained by its original medium-weight, single-engine design, the F-16V faces inherent gaps versus heavy fighters in range, payload, and upgrade potential, Song explained. The expert pointed out that what decides victory or defeat is no longer the performance of individual aircraft, but the entire combat system behind them. Modern warfare is no longer a matter of "soldier versus soldier, general versus general." The PLA's advantage lies in its comprehensively overwhelming system-of-systems combat capability. It is not necessary to shoot down an F-16V in the air, it can also be destroyed on the ground, by striking its shelters or cratering runways so that it cannot take off or land, Song said. The F-16V does improve Taiwan region's individual aircraft capabilities, but once integrated into a system-of-systems combat environment, its ability to alter the overall situation is extremely limited, said Song. A Xinhua News Agency report in March 2026 described how a certain PLA Air Force unit organized its three mainstay fighters, the J-20, J-16 and J-10C, to conduct multi-day-and-night air combat confrontation training covering situation sharing, coordinated strikes, electromagnetic countermeasures, and other subjects. The Taiwan regional authorities' attempt to rely on these F-16Vs to "resist reunification by force" is no different from a mantis trying to stop a chariot, Song said. From August 5 to 14, the Taiwan regional authorities conducted this year's "Han Kuang" military exercises. A CCTV News report on August 14 noted that the Taiwan region's Han Kuang exercises have become an annual farce. The entire exercise was plagued by continuous controversies. The so-called "Han Kuang" exercises have always been a hollow, wasteful spectacle. The Democratic Progressive Party authorities are hereby warned: the "Taiwan independence" dead end leads nowhere and cannot be altered. The PLA remains on high alert around the clock, continuously enhancing its combat readiness against separatist and external interference activities. It is, and will always be, the solid foundation for safeguarding national sovereignty and territorial integrity, and for maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Straits, Senior Colonel Chen Xi, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, said on August 14.

item.title: China's robots: Don't just watch, understand the industrial system
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 20:48:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT A Chinese humanoid robot clocked 9.39 seconds to beat the men's 100m world record of 9.58 seconds set by Usain Bolt. This feat, achieved during the opening ceremony of the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, quickly captured global headlines. The second World Humanoid Robot Games offered a vivid window into the country's fast-moving robotics industry. Images of humanoid machines running, balancing, navigating obstacles and performing coordinated tasks naturally attract attention. Such events reveal something significant: China has become exceptionally capable of translating advances in components, controls, software integration and manufacturing into physical machines that can be built, tested and improved at speed. The value of these competitions lies less in a single headline-grabbing performance than in the industrial system behind it. A humanoid robot on a track is the visible result of motors, reducers, sensors, batteries, structural materials, motion-control systems, embedded software, training data, assembly processes and field maintenance working together. China's advantage increasingly lies in its ability to coordinate the entire supply chain. It has a broad base of electronics and machinery suppliers, strong manufacturing capacity, dense industrial clusters, and a large pool of potential users willing to test robots in factories, warehouses, ports, shops, hospitals and service settings. Competitions can therefore serve as public demonstrations and stress tests for a wider ecosystem. This development has occurred amid expanding US restrictions on China's access to advanced technologies, particularly leading-edge semiconductors, high-performance computing equipment and certain software and manufacturing tools. These measures have had real effects. They raise costs, complicate supply chains and make it harder for Chinese firms to obtain some of the most advanced chips and technical capabilities. Robotics increasingly depends on artificial intelligence, high-performance processors and sophisticated development tools, and US containment policy has challenged China's robotics development. Yet the restrictions have not stopped China's robotics industry from growing. One reason is that industrial competitiveness is not determined by frontier chips alone. In many robotics applications, the decisive challenge is making a system reliable, affordable, maintainable and safe in real operating conditions. China's large and varied domestic market provides companies with unusually frequent opportunities to confront these challenges. A robot deployed in a logistics center, manufacturing workshop or pharmacy generates feedback that can improve design, software, hardware integration and service procedures. This creates a reinforcing cycle: More applications produce more operational data and experience; better products reduce costs and increase confidence; and lower costs support wider deployment. Scale matters as well. China's manufacturing ecosystem enables firms to move from prototype to small-batch production and then to larger-scale delivery relatively quickly. That process can accelerate learning not only for robot makers but also for suppliers of actuators, sensors, machine vision systems, batteries and precision components. The result is not simply a lower-cost version of foreign technology. It is a growing capacity to adapt products to diverse use cases and to iterate rapidly when products encounter real-world constraints. This has implications beyond China. As robots become more available and affordable, they can help manufacturers globally address labor shortages, improve workplace safety and raise productivity in repetitive or hazardous tasks. Chinese firms can contribute equipment, components and competitive pressure that expand the overall market and reduce barriers to adoption. In this sense, China's robotics progress may become part of a broader modernization of global manufacturing rather than a purely national achievement. However, a balanced assessment requires acknowledging the remaining gaps. The US retains major strengths in foundational artificial intelligence research, advanced semiconductors, computing platforms and software ecosystems. Japan and several European countries remain highly competitive in precision components, industrial reliability, specialized automation, safety systems and technical standards. China still faces challenges in certain high-end chips, core software, advanced sensors, precision parts, long-term reliability, and internationally recognized standards and certification. China's recent robotics events deserve attention because they illustrate a broader industrial fact. Despite external technological constraints, China has leveraged its domestic market, supply-chain depth, engineering talent and manufacturing scale to strengthen its position in robotics. Its advantage lies not in claiming technological supremacy in every category, but in its growing ability to turn innovation into deployment. If China can continue to close its remaining gaps while remaining open to global collaboration and standards, its robotics industry could become an important contributor to the next phase of worldwide industrial development.

item.title: Exclusive: Chinese ambassador hails mutual support as Colombian public expresses gratitude for China's earthquake relief aid
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 19:21:00
Photo: Chinese Embassy in Colombia Following the earthquake in Colombia earlier this month, the Chinese government has delivered emergency humanitarian earthquake relief supplies to the country. Chinese Ambassador to Colombia Zhu Jingyang told the Global Times on Saturday that the two countries' support in the face of natural disasters vividly embodies the spirit of a community with a shared future for humanity. A magnitude-7.5 earthquake struck northwestern Colombia on August 10, according to China Earthquake Networks Center, with 32 cities severely affected. Chinese Embassy in Colombia said that the emergency humanitarian relief supplies provided by the Chinese government arrived at El Dorado International Airport in Bogota at noon on August 18. The roughly 80-ton shipment included generators, water purification vehicles, disinfection equipment, solar lighting equipment, tents and blankets. Chinese Ambassador to Colombia Zhu told the Global Times on Saturday that the hardest-hit areas faced complex challenges. Choco, the epicenter, is one of Colombia's least-developed regions, making reconstruction difficult. Valle del Cauca, the country's second-most populous department, was widely affected. Pereira, capital of Risaralda, suffered numerous building collapses and the highest death toll. "Our embassy has tailored and carefully organized the relief effort, and the humanitarian supplies provided by the Chinese government have been delivered to the Colombian side," Zhu said. With strong assistance from COSCO Shipping, the embassy worked with Colombian authorities to transport and distribute the supplies to victims in Valle del Cauca. Heavy machinery from Chinese companies arrived in Pereira shortly after the earthquake to assist with rescue and debris clearance, while Chinese companies in Colombia spontaneously donated and transported supplies to Choco, ensuring Chinese assistance reached all major disaster areas, and fully demonstrating China's humanitarian care and its sense of responsibility as a major country, Zhu introduced. China's relief efforts drew an enthusiastic response in Colombia. Zhu said that, according to incomplete statistics, most major Colombian media outlets and several major international media extensively covered China's cash and emergency humanitarian assistance. Posts on the embassy's social media accounts have garnered nearly 8 million views. Many Colombians spontaneously expressed their gratitude, while regional media, self-media and opinion leaders produced articles, graphics and videos promoting China's relief efforts and calling for the new government to strengthen cooperation with China and safeguard bilateral friendship. "Recognition from the Colombian people shows that China-Colombia friendship is deeply rooted in people's hearts," Zhu said. "Strengthening bilateral cooperation has become a consensus across regions and sectors. China-Colombia ties are not affected by changes of government, and the two countries' support in the face of natural disasters vividly embodies the spirit of a community with a shared future for humanity, where nations stand together through storms and share weal and woe." Zhu also cited a Pew survey showing public favorability toward China among Colombians has reached a record high. Photo: Chinese Embassy in Colombia Meanwhile, the safety of Chinese nationals in Colombia remains the embassy's top concern. Immediately after the earthquake, the embassy activated its emergency response mechanism and, despite disrupted communications and transportation, conducted multiple rounds of checks on Chinese citizens, Chinese-funded institutions and overseas Chinese communities. So far, no Chinese nationals have been reported injured or killed. On the day of the earthquake, the embassy also received an urgent request from the Hong Kong SAR government to help locate a Hong Kong resident's family that had lost contact in Cali, Zhu said. Despite communications disruptions, the embassy contacted them within hours and confirmed they were safe. After some Chinese-owned shops reported collapsed or cracked exterior walls, the embassy organized community groups to conduct targeted assessments and aid. It also issued multiple consular advisories, urging Chinese nationals to avoid non-essential travel to affected areas and guard against aftershocks, health hazards and other secondary risks. In the interview, Zhu urged Chinese nationals in Colombia and those planning to visit to remain vigilant, noting the country's serious security situation and successive natural disasters, including earthquakes, forest fires and volcanic eruptions. He also urged them to avoid complacency, noting that one department remains at extremely high risk and 18 other remain at high risk, strengthen safety precautions and emergency preparedness.

item.title: China, Arab states launch a five-year action plan to combat drought, desertification and land degradation
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 17:14:00
Picture of desert in Aswan, Egypt: VCG China and Arab states have launched a five-year action plan to combat drought, desertification and land degradation, which expand their cooperation beyond traditional desertification control to technological innovation in areas such as grassland conservation, watershed management and wetland protection, during a UN conference in combating desertification, the Global Times learned from China's National Forestry and Grassland Administration (NFGA) on Sunday. The plan was launched at a meeting on the sidelines of the 17th session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (COP17), now underway in Ulan Bator, Mongolia. Under the action plan, China and Arab states will deepen practical cooperation over the next five years in key areas including desertification and degraded land restoration, sand and dust storm monitoring and early warning, grassland management, biodiversity conservation, and wetland protection and restoration, according to a press release sent to the Global Times by the NFGA. The two sides will step up technological innovation and the application of research outcomes by developing platforms for sharing technologies, data and research results, conducting interdisciplinary research, and developing technologies such as remote sensing and intelligent assessment of land degradation. The plan also calls for establishing demonstration bases supporting the implementation of the UN Convention to Combat Desertification. The plan also calls for strengthening China-Arab cooperation networks on desertification control, improving mechanisms for sharing policies, technologies and research outcomes, and expanding partnerships under the China-proposed Belt and Road Initiative. Governments, research institutions, businesses, social organizations and local communities will be encouraged to participate. Cooperation on capacity building will also be expanded through exchanges among young experts, joint research, field demonstrations and technical training. The meeting was jointly hosted by China's NFGA and the Secretariat of the League of Arab States, and organized by the Chinese Academy of Forestry and the China-Arab States International Research Center for Drought, Desertification and Land Degradation. Cui Lijuan, vice president of the Chinese Academy of Forestry noted that some initiatives are already taking shape. China and Egypt, for example, are exploring a comparative study of the basins of Yellow River and Nile River, with the aim of exchanging experience in ecological protection and integrated watershed management. The initiative, according to Cui, has received support from the Chinese Academy of Forestry and attracted interest from international non-governmental organizations. Future cooperation between China and Arab states will also focus on desertification monitoring and early warning, ecological technologies, and exchanges and training for young professionals. The two sides also aim to broaden participation by bringing businesses, social organizations and international institutions into a cooperation framework currently led primarily by government agencies, Cui said. In 2023, the China-Arab International Research Center on Drought, Desertification and Land Degradation was inaugurated during an international forum on desert control, showcasing China's commitment to sharing its expertise gained from the Kubuqi desert control, per Xinhua. Over the past three years, the center has steadily strengthened regular cooperation mechanisms between China and Arab states. The two sides have jointly developed Earth observation and intelligent decision-support tools for land degradation, while China has compiled 30 practical desertification-control technologies across six categories suitable for application in Arab states, according to NFGA. The center has also established regular channels of exchange with countries including Saudi Arabia and Egypt, while building an initial China-Arab desertification-control network and expert pool to support continued technical cooperation and professional training across Arab states.

item.title: Chinese authorities order local probe, nationwide market check over wholesaler using formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh: report
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23 12:45:00
Photo: Screenshot from an online blogger's video Following reports circulating online about the use of formaldehyde solution during bulk purchases and transportation of cabbages and county-level authorities in North China's Hebei Province confirming its illegal use, Chinese relevant authorities have promptly guided local authorities to conduct investigations, according to CCTV News on Sunday. The office of the food safety commission of the State Council, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, and the State Administration for Market Regulation have instructed local authorities to conduct investigations, handling the incident strictly and expeditiously in accordance with the law, trace the distribution of the implicated cabbages, and prevent problematic products from entering the market. In addition, local governments nationwide have also been urged to immediately carry out special sampling inspections and market checks on perishable vegetables such as cabbage. Any violations of laws and regulations discovered will be severely punished without leniency, the report noted. County-level authorities in North China's Hebei Province have confirmed its illegal use to preserve freshness after a preliminary investigation, according to a statement on Saturday. Police have taken legal compulsory measures against the individuals involved and the vehicles concerned, and the case is under further investigation, according to a statement by local authorities on Saturday. According to The Paper, a blogger posted a video on August 22 claiming that, in Kangbao county of Zhangjiakou, several batches of cabbages were randomly selected for inspection, and all were found to have been dipped in formaldehyde solution before being loaded onto trucks to preserve their freshness. The statement by authorities in Kangbao county on the same day noted that authorities immediately organized relevant departments, including those responsible for agriculture and rural affairs, market regulation, and public security authorities, to conduct an on-site investigation. A preliminary investigation has confirmed that the situation shown in the video is genuine. The incident involved the wholesaler illegally using formaldehyde solution during the loading and transportation of vegetables in an attempt to preserve their freshness. The public security authorities have taken legal compulsory measures against the individuals involved and the relevant vehicles. The case is currently under further investigation, per the statement. At the same time, authorities are urgently tracing the distribution and destination of the affected cabbages. The county is also conducting a comprehensive inspection of vegetable purchasing, transportation, and sales activities to identify and address similar violations. "Any illegal or non-compliant practices discovered will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law to ensure the safety of the vegetable supply," the statement read. In an attempt to improve the appearance of the cabbages and reduce losses during transportation, the wholesalers took the risk of using formaldehyde to preserve them. The nature of the violation is extremely serious and utterly absurd, according to a commentary article published by People's Daily on Saturday. China's Law on Food Safety and on Quality and Safety of Agricultural Products stipulate that the use of freshness-preserving agents, preservatives and other substances in the packaging, preservation, storage and transportation of agricultural products must comply with national food safety standards. Formaldehyde, classified as a Group 1 carcinogen, is strictly prohibited from being added or used. "The wholesalers focused solely on their immediate economic interests while completely disregarding the lives and health of consumers have crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line, while also damaging the good reputation of local agricultural products and causing innocent losses to local farmers who comply with regulations," People's Daily wrote. item.title: China's upgraded high-altitude wind power project that extracts clean energy from stratosphere completes test
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22 11:17:00
Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News China's high-altitude wind power technology has achieved a major breakthrough, as the domestically developed S4000 Stratosphere Airborne Wind Energy System (SAWES) recently completed a test at a base in Northwest China, CCTV News reported on Saturday. An upgraded version of the earlier S2000 SAWES, and the successful completion of its full-process flight validation marks the transition of China's stratospheric high-altitude wind power technology from the iterative development phase toward the engineering deployment phase, according to the report. The test covered the entire process of ascent, station‑keeping, power generation testing, and smooth recovery, with all indicators meeting the required standards, fully verifying the system's reliability in complex and extreme high‑altitude environments, the report said. As an upgrade from the S2000 model, the S4000 adopts a new configuration with significantly improved overall performance. Its maximum operational altitude reaches 4,000 meters, making it suitable for deployment in the vast majority of regions across China. It can directly adapt to mainstream grid power supply requirements and has a design service life of up to 20 years. Unlike conventional low-altitude wind turbines, which are often referred to as "windmills," the system employs a flying device. Global Times
